implementation_notes: Keep the field unexported (`courses []Course`) so no other package can touch it, and return a fresh slice - `slices.Clone(p.courses)` or `append([]Course(nil), p.courses...)` - because handing out the slice header there and then hands out the backing array: a caller can overwrite elements or append into shared capacity. Membership changes go through pointer-receiver methods `AddCourse`/`RemoveCourse` that own validation and any derived state. The copy is cheap (one allocation for the element references) and shallow; it is the default for small in-memory collections.
pitfalls: Returning `p.courses` directly leaks the backing array: `p.Courses()[0] = x` or an append into shared capacity silently rewrites the owner's data.
The copy is shallow - Course values containing pointers, maps or slices keep sharing those internals with the original.
Value receivers copy the struct (and thus the slice header) but not the array: a mutating method on a value receiver that appends is lost work - use pointer receivers for the mutators.

variants.name: range-over-func iterator (iter.Seq, Go 1.23)
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23's range-over-func iterators expose traversal without materialising or aliasing the backing slice: the method returns an `iter.Seq[Course]` whose yield callback is driven by `for c := range p.Courses()`. The go.dev announcement frames the feature exactly this way - for/range accesses elements 'without exposing the underlying representation' - and it composes with slices.Collect, slices.Sorted and iter.Pull for callers that do need a slice or a pull loop. Keep the copied-slice accessor when callers need len(), random access or a value they can sort/store; choose iterators for large, lazy or streamed sequences.
pitfalls: Yield must respect early termination: calling yield again after it returned false panics ('range function continued iteration after function call returned false').
Mutating membership while a caller ranges over the iterator is a data race on the slice header - the iterator is not a snapshot and offers no protection.
Iterators hide the concrete backing array but not element aliasing: yielding Course values copies them only if Course is a value type without pointer fields.
Do not wrap a small in-memory slice in iter.Seq for fashion: the closure and indirect calls cost more than returning a slice when the collection already fits in memory.
